rationale: The imperative "שְׁתֵה מַ֥יִם" (oshb:Prov.5.15; “Drink water”, web:Prov.5.15) opens a positive counterpart to the preceding warning: instead of the stranger's door (5:8), the addressee is directed to his own cistern, well, and spring (5:15-17), then to bless that spring and “Rejoice in the wife of your youth” (web:Prov.5.18), closing with the doe/deer figure of 5:19. The unit is bounded by a change of addressee-object (from the adulteress to the wife) and grammatical mood (from prohibition to affirmative imperative and blessing), and closes before 5:20 pivots back to an interrogative warning.
rejected_alternative: Folding 5:15-19 into the unit that follows was rejected because 5:20 shifts from affirmative imperative and blessing to an interrogative warning, a distinct rhetorical mode addressed to a different object.

The closing verb of this span, תִּשְׁגֶּ֥ה (root shagah, oshb:Prov.5.19), recurs as the opening verb of the following row's rhetorical question, תִשְׁגֶּ֣ה (oshb:Prov.5.20) -- disclosed as a lexical seam link, consistent with the register-shift boundary argued above.

rationale: The rhetorical question "וְלָ֤מָּה תִשְׁגֶּ֣ה בְנִ֣י..." (oshb:Prov.5.20; “why should you, my son, be captivated...”, web:Prov.5.20) reopens direct address with the vocative recurring as the third word of the verse (not verse-initial, unlike the unit-opening occurrences at 5:1 and 6:1). The unit moves from the question (5:20) to a Yahweh-observation clause (5:21, “the ways of man are before Yahweh's eyes”, web:Prov.5.21) to the wicked man's self-entrapment by his own iniquities (5:22) and his death for lack of instruction (5:23), one question-to-consequence argument that the petuchah at oshb:Prov.5.23 marks off as its own unit.
rejected_alternative: Isolating 5:21 as its own one-verse row for its Yahweh-clause was rejected because the argument needs the self-entrapment and death clauses of 5:22-23 to complete, clauses that the petuchah at oshb:Prov.5.23 closes.

rationale: "לֵֽךְ אֶל נְמָלָ֥ה עָצֵ֑ל..." (oshb:Prov.6.6; “Go to the ant, you sluggard”, web:Prov.6.6) opens a second-person imperative address built on an observed-nature example: the ant's self-directed provision without overseer (6.7-8) is set against a rhetorical question to the sluggard (“How long will you sleep...”, web:Prov.6.9) and a mimicked quotation of his own procrastination (6:10), closing with the consequence of poverty arriving “as a robber” (web:Prov.6.11). The governing verbs stay second-person imperative and interrogative across the unit, distinct from the third-person participial portrait that opens at 6:12.
rejected_alternative: Splitting 6:7-6:8's third-person ant description from the second-person frame at 6:6/6:9-6:11 was rejected because the third-person material functions as embedded illustration inside the second-person admonition framing it on both sides with direct address to the sluggard, not as an independent voice-shift seam.

rationale: "נְצֹ֣ר בְּ֭נִי מִצְוַ֣ת אָבִ֑יךָ..." (oshb:Prov.6.20; “My son, keep your father's commandment”, web:Prov.6.20) reopens the lecture-frame vocative that reappears here after 6:1. The unit binds the commandment to the body (6:21, tied on the heart, bound on the neck) and to a light-metaphor: "נֵ֣ר מִ֭צְוָה וְת֣וֹרָה א֑וֹר" (oshb:Prov.6.23; “the commandment is a lamp, and the law is light”, web:Prov.6.23), closing on “the way of life” (web:Prov.6.23). That closing figure completes the metaphor opened at 6:20-21 before 6:24 pivots to a purpose clause naming a specific new threat, the adulteress, not yet in view in 6:20-23.
rejected_alternative: Extending this unit through 6:26 was reconsidered because the infinitive-of-purpose opening 6:24 is the grammatical continuation of 6:23's motive clause rather than an independently introduced addressee-threat; the resulting 6:23/6:24 seam lacks a vocative-restart of its own, and the parashah layer stays silent there too, with the nearest petuchah marks sitting at oshb:Prov.6.19, before this unit, and oshb:Prov.6.26, inside the following material.

rationale: The infinitive-of-purpose clause "לִ֭שְׁמָרְךָ מֵאֵ֣שֶׁת רָ֑ע..." (oshb:Prov.6.24; “to keep you from the immoral woman”, web:Prov.6.24) governs the whole span: it states the aim, 6:25 issues the matching prohibition (do not lust after her beauty), 6:26 supplies the causal warrant (a prostitute reduces you to a loaf of bread), and 6:27-28 supply a paired rhetorical-question analogy (fire in the lap, walking on coals) that 6:29 applies directly back to the purpose clause's subject: "כֵּ֗ן הַ֭בָּא אֶל אֵ֣שֶׁת רֵעֵ֑הוּ..." (oshb:Prov.6.29; “So is he who goes in to his neighbor's wife”, web:Prov.6.29). The unit closes there, before 6:30 opens an unrelated comparison subject, the thief. This governing infinitive-of-purpose is itself the syntactic continuation of the preceding row's closing motive clause at 6:23 (oshb:Prov.6.23), not an independently introduced topic; the resulting 6:23/6:24 seam lacks a vocative-restart of its own, and the parashah layer stays silent there too, with the nearest petuchah marks sitting at oshb:Prov.6.19, before the unit, and oshb:Prov.6.26, inside this row's own span.
rejected_alternative: Splitting the fire-and-coals rhetorical questions (6:27-29) into their own row was rejected because they supply the warrant for the prohibition of 6:24-26 under one governing purpose clause, not an independent topic. The petuchah at 6:26 is disclosed as tier-3 corroboration for a possible 6:20-26/6:27-35 split, but the governing purpose infinitive opened at 6:24 argues against treating 6:26 as the operative seam.

rationale: "לֹא יָב֣וּזוּ לַ֭גַּנָּב..." (oshb:Prov.6.30; “Men don't despise a thief...”, web:Prov.6.30) opens a new comparison subject: a thief who steals from hunger draws some social allowance and owes restitution (6:30-31), but the adulterer, unlike the thief, “is void of understanding” and “destroys his own soul” (web:Prov.6.32), facing wounds, dishonor, and a husband's unrelenting jealousy that “won't spare in the day of vengeance” and “won't regard any ransom” (web:Prov.6.34-35). The a fortiori argument (lesser case, thief, versus greater case, adulterer) is confined to these six verses and closes the chapter at the petuchah of 6:35, before the next lecture reopens at 7:1 outside this part.
rejected_alternative: Reading 6:30-35 as a single_proverb was rejected because the thief-versus-adulterer comparison unfolds across paired clauses building one a fortiori argument, not one couplet; treating it as a numerical_saying was also rejected, since no x-of-y count governs the span.
